scenario.title: Senior Backend Engineer: John vs. Sally
scenario.brief: The panel must recommend exactly one candidate for a senior backend role on a payments team. Each panelist attended different parts of the interview loop and holds different evidence.

candidates.name: John
candidates.blurb: Polished, confident, eight years of Go

candidates.name: Sally
candidates.blurb: Nervous in the panel, has never written Go

agents.name: Dana
agents.style: direct and decisive; wants to close the loop

agents.name: Priya
agents.style: warm, focused on references and team fit

agents.name: Tom
agents.style: skeptical, asks what could go wrong

facts.text: Sally single-handedly designed and shipped the ledger migration at her last company, moving 2B rows with zero downtime.
Four engineers Sally mentored were promoted within two years; two now lead teams.
Sally wrote the incident-postmortem process that her whole org adopted; her former director calls it the most valuable thing anyone did that year.
In the debugging session Sally found a silent data-loss bug in our sample legacy service in under 20 minutes, including the race that caused it.
Sally's system design answer correctly anticipated the double-spend failure mode and proposed idempotency keys before being prompted.
Sally's back-channel reference, a former skip-level, says Sally is the person they would hire first for an ambiguous, under-specified problem.
Sally drove an infrastructure cost reduction of 40% by rewriting the batch settlement job, and documented it so others could repeat it.
Sally maintains a small open-source Postgres migration tool with a few hundred stars.
Sally's written design sample was clear and well-structured.
Sally was visibly nervous in the panel round and rambled through two answers before recovering.
Sally has never written Go, which is our primary backend language.
Sally's most recent tenure was only 14 months.
Sally declined to use the whiteboard and asked to work in an editor instead.
Sally has no formal management experience and no direct reports.
John gave a polished, confident panel performance and answered every behavioural question crisply.
John has eight years of Go, our primary backend language.
John led a team of six engineers at his last company.
John comes from a top-tier, brand-name employer that everyone on the panel recognises.
John's take-home was submitted fast and the code was clean and idiomatic.
John already knows the fintech domain and used our vocabulary correctly throughout.
John is available to start immediately.
John's back-channel reference says three of his six reports left within a year, two citing John directly in exit interviews.
John's take-home is near-identical to a public blog post solution, down to variable names and an unusual comment.
John was openly dismissive of the QA engineer on the panel, talking over them twice.
John claimed to have 'led the platform migration'; his former colleague says John was one of twelve contributors and did not lead it.
John refused to discuss a production outage he owned, calling it 'not really mine'.
In the closing round John asked only about title and compensation and no questions about the product or users.
This would be John's third role in four years, each exit abrupt and mid-project.
